studies.Reference: Tea consumption and ovarian cancer risk in a population-based cohort.
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Participants completed a validated 67-item food frequency questionnaire at enrollment between 1987 and 1990

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 61 057 women aged 40 to 76 years who were participants in the population-based Swedish Mammography Cohort
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Each additional cup of tea per day was associated with an 18% lower risk of ovarian cancer (multivariate hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.68-0.99)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Tea consumption was inversely associated with the risk of ovarian cancer after controlling for potential confounders
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: 301 incident cases of invasive epithelial ovarian cancer were ascertained
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: tea consumption measured by validated 67-item food frequency questionnaire; categories: never/seldom, <1 cup/day, 1 cup/day, ≥2 cups/day

studies.Reference: Consumption of black tea or coffee and risk of ovarian cancer.
studies.Authors: Baker JA, Boakye K, McCann SE, Beehler GP, Rodabaugh KJ, Villella JA, Moysich KB
studies.Journal: International journal of gynecological cancer : official journal of the International Gynecological Cancer Society
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: All participants completed a comprehensive epidemiologic questionnaire. Black tea consumption was associated with a linear decline in ovarian cancer risk.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: participants included 414 women with primary epithelial ovarian, fallopian, or peritoneal cancer and 868 age- and region-matched women with nonneoplastic conditions
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: individuals consuming two or more cups daily experiencing a 30% decline in risk (adjusted OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.51-0.97)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Black tea consumption was associated with a linear decline in ovarian cancer risk
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: 414 women with primary epithelial ovarian, fallopian, or peritoneal cancer
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Black tea consumption... individuals consuming two or more cups daily

studies.Reference: Coffee, tea and caffeine and risk of epithelial ovarian cancer.
studies.Authors: Jordan SJ, Purdie DM, Green AC, Webb PM
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Women provided comprehensive reproductive and lifestyle data and completed a food frequency questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Women with epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) (n = 696) and control women selected from the Electoral Roll (n = 786)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: tea consumption was not related to EOC (OR: 1.10 95% CI: 0.76-1.61 for >/=4 cups/day versus none)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: tea consumption was not related to EOC
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.619.

studies.Reference: Tea, coffee, and caffeinated beverage consumption and risk of epithelial ovarian cancers.
studies.Authors: Leung AC, Cook LS, Swenerton K, Gilks B, Gallagher RP, Magliocco A, Steed H, Köbel M, Nation J, Brooks-Wilson A, Le ND
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Adult lifetime cumulative consumption (cup-years=cups/day*years) was calculated. Those that did not meet the threshold for beverage consumption (at least once per month for 6 months or more) were classified as non-drinkers.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: there were a total of 524 cases and 1587 controls
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: there was an increase in risk in black tea only drinkers (aOR=1.56; 95% CI:1.07-2.28 for >40 cup-years)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Black tea consumption may be associated with an increased risk epithelial ovarian carcinoma
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.021.
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: After restricting to cases of epithelial invasive cancers and controls aged 40-79 years
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: tea (black/caffeinated tea and green tea separately), Adult lifetime cumulative consumption (cup-years=cups/day*years) was calculated

studies.Reference: Tea consumption reduces ovarian cancer risk.
studies.Authors: Lee AH, Su D, Pasalich M, Binns CW
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Information on frequency, quantity and duration of tea drinking, amount of dried tea leaves brewed, together with habitual diet and lifestyle characteristics, was obtained face-to-face from participants using a validated and reliable questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Five hundred incident patients with histologically confirmed epithelial carcinoma of the ovary and 500 controls (mean age 59 years) were recruited
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Regular drinking of green tea, black tea and/or oolong tea was associated with a lower risk of ovarian cancer, the adjusted odds ratio being 0.29
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Regular drinking of green tea, black tea and/or oolong tea was associated with a lower risk of ovarian cancer. Regular tea consumption is associated with a reduced risk of ovarian cancer
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: apparent inverse dose-response relationships were observed for years of drinking, number of cups and quantity of tea consumed, as well as amount of dried tea leaves brewed (p < 0.01)
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: adjusted odds ratio being 0.29 (95% confidence interval 0.22-0.39)
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: Five hundred incident patients with histologically confirmed epithelial carcinoma of the ovary
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: Information on frequency, quantity and duration of tea drinking, amount of dried tea leaves brewed. Regular drinking of green tea, black tea and/or oolong tea

studies.Reference: A prospective study of dietary flavonoid intake and incidence of epithelial ovarian cancer.
studies.Authors: Gates MA, Tworoger SS, Hecht JL, De Vivo I, Rosner B, Hankinson SE
studies.comparison_type: Highest vs Lowest quintile (kaempferol intake, primary contributor: tea)
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: We calculated each participant's intake of myricetin, kaempferol, quercetin, luteolin and apigenin from dietary data collected at multiple time points. There was evidence of an inverse association with consumption of tea (nonherbal) and broccoli, the primary contributors to kaempferol intake in our population.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 66,940 women in the Nurses' Health Study
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: significant 40% decrease in ovarian cancer incidence for the highest versus lowest quintile of kaempferol intake (RR = 0.60, 95% CI = 0.42-0.87; p-trend = 0.002)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: There was evidence of an inverse association with consumption of tea (nonherbal) and broccoli, the primary contributors to kaempferol intake in our population
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: incidence of epithelial ovarian cancer. Our analysis included 347 cases diagnosed between 1984 and 2002
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: consumption of tea (nonherbal) and broccoli, the primary contributors to kaempferol intake in our population

studies.Reference: Intake of dietary flavonoids and risk of epithelial ovarian cancer.
studies.Authors: Cassidy A, Huang T, Rice MS, Rimm EB, Tworoger SS
studies.Journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
studies.comparison_type: >1 cup black tea/d vs ≤1 cup black tea/d
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Intake was calculated from validated food-frequency questionnaires collected every 4 y.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: We followed 171,940 Nurses' Health Study and Nurses' Health Study II participants
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: In food-based analyses used to compare subjects who consumed >1 and ≤ 1 cup black tea/d, the HR was 0.68 (95% CI: 0.51, 0.90; P < 0.01)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Higher intakes of flavonols and flavanones as well as black tea consumption may be associated with lower risk of ovarian cancer
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: During 16-22 y of follow-up, 723 cases of ovarian cancer were confirmed through medical records
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: In food-based analyses used to compare subjects who consumed >1 and ≤ 1 cup black tea/d

studies.Reference: Lifetime caffeine intake and the risk of epithelial ovarian cancer.
studies.Authors: Grundy A, Sandhu S, Arseneau J, Gilbert L, Gotlieb WH, Aronson KJ, Koushik A
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: lifetime intake of caffeinated coffee, black tea, green tea and cola sodas was assessed and used to calculate lifetime total intake of caffeine

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Among 497 cases and 904 controls in a population-based case-control study
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: The OR (95% CI) of ovarian cancer for the highest versus lowest quartile of lifetime caffeine intake was 1.17 (0.83-1.64)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: Lifetime caffeine intake was not strongly associated with ovarian cancer risk
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: Computed from the reported effect and 95% CI using a normal approximation: p=0.366.
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: The OR (95% CI) of ovarian cancer for the highest versus lowest quartile of lifetime caffeine intake was 1.17 (0.83-1.64)
extraction_supporting_text.outcome_definition: ovarian cancer risk overall, as well as by menopausal status. Multivariable polytomous logistic regression was used to estimate the associations for invasive and borderline ovarian cancers separately
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: lifetime intake of caffeinated coffee, black tea, green tea and cola sodas was assessed and used to calculate lifetime total intake of caffeine

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.9260). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 6 studies yielded an effect size of 0.77 (95% CI: 0.53–1.13), indicating no statistically significant association between tea and ovarian cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 91.92%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
